options.a: Checked to ensure they open/close properly and warning devices work as required
options.b: Kept latched with the release covers sealed so passengers cannot open them in transit
options.c: Verified only by confirming the exit signs are lit; opening them is left to maintenance
options.d: Checked from outside for damage, with the opening test done monthly instead of daily

distractorExplanations.b: Exits must be operable from inside; sealing the release covers defeats emergency egress and is itself a defect, not a precaution.
distractorExplanations.c: Lit signs do not prove an exit works; the driver confirms the exits open and close and the warning buzzers function.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a periodic maintenance check with the pre-trip; emergency exit operation and alarms are verified before each trip.

options.a: Federal rules require brake checks only on buses traveling over 55 mph on interstates
options.b: Stopping distance and passenger safety depend on properly functioning service and parking brakes
options.c: Bus brakes are checked mainly so the parking brake can hold the bus at loading stops
options.d: A pre-trip brake check replaces the need to monitor brake response and air pressure en route

distractorExplanations.a: Invents a speed and road threshold; brake checks are part of every pre-trip whatever the route or speed of the bus.
distractorExplanations.c: Covers only one use of one brake; the check matters because service brakes govern stopping distance with a full passenger load.
distractorExplanations.d: A pre-trip check does not substitute for watching gauges and brake response while driving; defects can develop during the trip.

options.a: Note it on the post-trip report and run the route, since interior lights are not safety items
options.b: Run daytime trips and repair it before the first route that operates after sunset
options.c: Address the defect per out-of-service / company rules before operating with passengers
options.d: Have passengers stay seated for the trip, which makes the missing light acceptable

distractorExplanations.a: Aisle lighting needed for safe movement is passenger safety equipment; deferring it to the post-trip leaves riders at risk now.
distractorExplanations.b: Assumes the defect matters only at night; tunnels, dim interiors and evacuations still need working aisle lights, so repair comes first.
distractorExplanations.d: Keeping riders seated does not cure a lighting defect; they still board, alight and may need to evacuate, so the defect is addressed first.

options.a: Stored in a cargo bay so it stays secured away from passengers
options.b: Present and charged, with the gauge read only at annual inspection
options.c: Required on buses over 26 passengers, optional on smaller coaches
options.d: Present, charged/sealed as required, and readily accessible

distractorExplanations.a: A cargo-bay extinguisher is not readily accessible to the driver during a fire; it must be mounted where it can be reached at once.
distractorExplanations.b: The charge gauge and seal are part of every pre-trip check, not just the annual inspection; a discharged unit could go unnoticed.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a seating threshold; every bus carries a properly rated, charged extinguisher as required emergency equipment.

options.a: A serious defect that may place the vehicle out of service
options.b: Acceptable until the next scheduled service if the crack is under 6 inches
options.c: A cosmetic issue to note on the post-trip report for later repair
options.d: A concern mainly if it is on the passenger side of the windshield

distractorExplanations.b: Invents a length allowance; damage in the driver's critical vision area is a serious defect that can put the bus out of service now.
distractorExplanations.c: Damage in the critical vision area impairs the driver's sight line; it is a safety defect, not a cosmetic post-trip note.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the risk: the driver's side wiper sweep is the critical vision zone, so a crack there is the serious case.

options.a: Hydraulic fluid level only, since the lift is checked by maintenance
options.b: Proper operation, damage, and required securement belts/devices
options.c: Lift operation, with tiedowns and belts left to the rider to bring
options.d: A check done on days a wheelchair rider is scheduled for the route

distractorExplanations.a: Fluid level is one item; the driver must cycle the lift and confirm securement belts and devices are present and undamaged.
distractorExplanations.c: Securement belts and tiedowns are vehicle equipment the driver checks; riders are not responsible for supplying them.
distractorExplanations.d: Accessibility equipment is inspected on every pre-trip when equipped; unscheduled riders who need it may board at any stop.

options.a: Tread depth to at least 2/32 inch on steering tires, plus inflation checks
options.b: Inflation checked by thumping, with tread measured at oil changes
options.c: Tread depth, inflation, cuts/bulges, and dual matching as applicable
options.d: Inflation and tread, with recapped tires allowed on the front axle

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the 2/32-inch limit for other tires with the 4/32-inch minimum on steering-axle tires, and omits cuts and bulges.
distractorExplanations.b: Thumping does not measure pressure, and tread depth is a pre-trip item, not something left to a service interval.
distractorExplanations.d: Recapped, regrooved or retreaded tires are not allowed on the front wheels of a bus; this confuses the rear-axle allowance with the steer axle.

options.a: On board, but set out only after a stop lasting more than 30 minutes
options.b: Replaced by hazard flashers, which satisfy the warning rule by themselves
options.c: Carried in the depot truck that responds to breakdowns on the route
options.d: On board and available to set out during stops/breakdowns as required

distractorExplanations.a: Triangles go out as soon as possible, within 10 minutes of stopping, not after waiting half an hour.
distractorExplanations.b: Flashers are used immediately but do not replace the three reflective triangles required when stopped on a roadway or shoulder.
distractorExplanations.c: Warning devices must travel on the bus so the driver can deploy them right away; a support truck may arrive far too late.

options.a: Secure mounting and hazardous damage that could injure riders
options.b: Cushion wear and torn upholstery, which is the main seat-safety risk
options.c: Correct seat numbering so passengers can find assigned seats
options.d: Mounting bolts on the front row, where passengers stand up most

distractorExplanations.b: Upholstery wear is cosmetic; the safety check is that seats and stanchions are securely mounted with no broken or sharp parts.
distractorExplanations.c: Seat numbering is a customer-service item; the inspection targets loose mounts and damage that injure riders in a sudden stop.
distractorExplanations.d: Any seat or handhold in the cabin can come loose; checking just the front row misses hazards throughout the bus.

options.a: Drive to the shop at reduced speed, using the gauge in place of the alarm
options.b: Not operate until repaired—warning devices are critical safety systems
options.c: Proceed if the governor cuts in at 100 psi, which proves the alarm works
options.d: Report it on the post-trip inspection and repair it before the next day

distractorExplanations.a: Operating with a failed required warning is not permitted; the gauge does not replace the low-pressure alarm that must work.
distractorExplanations.c: Governor cut-in tests the compressor, not the low-air warning; the warning must activate before pressure falls below about 60 psi.
distractorExplanations.d: A failed low-air warning found on pre-trip must be repaired before carrying passengers, not deferred to the post-trip report.

options.a: Closed, with latching checked when baggage is loaded inside
options.b: Left unlocked during the trip so passengers can reach their bags
options.c: Securely closed/latched so items cannot fall onto the roadway
options.d: Closed by the passengers who loaded them, without a driver check

distractorExplanations.a: An unlatched empty door can still swing open at speed; latches are checked on every pre-trip, loaded or not.
distractorExplanations.b: Passengers do not access baggage compartments en route; doors stay secured so they cannot open while the bus is moving.
distractorExplanations.d: The driver remains responsible for confirming every compartment is latched before moving; it is not delegated to riders.

options.a: Present and adequately stocked/accessible
options.b: Kept at the terminal and issued on charter trips
options.c: Present, with restocking left until the annual audit
options.d: Stored in the baggage bay to free up cabin space

distractorExplanations.b: A first-aid kit required on the bus is carried on board for every trip, not issued from the terminal for charters.
distractorExplanations.c: A kit that is present but depleted fails the requirement; supplies are restocked when used, not at an annual audit.
distractorExplanations.d: An exterior baggage bay makes the kit inaccessible during an emergency inside the cabin; it must be reachable.

options.a: Normal wear that is acceptable until the next scheduled service
options.b: The vehicle may be unsafe/out of service until corrected
options.c: Safe to drive once power steering fluid is topped off before departure
options.d: A concern for tractor-trailers, but tolerable on a two-axle bus

distractorExplanations.a: Steering play beyond limits (more than about 10 degrees) is a safety defect that can be out of service now, not routine wear.
distractorExplanations.c: Adding fluid does not correct mechanical free play in the linkage or gear; play beyond the limit still needs repair first.
distractorExplanations.d: Steering limits apply to every CMV; a bus with loose steering and a load of passengers is at least as dangerous.

options.a: Fuel level and mileage, since defects are found on the pre-trip
options.b: Defects that caused a delay, leaving minor issues unreported
options.c: New defects, passenger damage, and items left behind
options.d: Passenger complaints, which replace a written condition report

distractorExplanations.a: Post-trip reports exist to capture defects found during the trip; leaving them to the next pre-trip loses that information.
distractorExplanations.b: Any defect affecting safety is reported, not just ones that delayed the route; small issues become failures.
distractorExplanations.d: Complaints can point to problems, but the driver still completes a vehicle condition report covering defects found.

cdl-passenger-readiness-check-vehicle-in.explanation: Post-trips catch defects early and protect the next passengers; damage and items left behind can affect the next trip's safety.

options.a: Remain behind the standee line and not obstruct the driver’s vision or controls
options.b: Stand anywhere forward of the rear axle so weight stays balanced
options.c: Stand in the stepwell when seats are full to keep the aisle clear
options.d: Remain seated whenever the bus exceeds 25 mph, standing only at slower speeds

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses weight distribution with the standee rule; standees stay behind the standee line, not just forward of an axle.
distractorExplanations.c: The stepwell is forward of the standee line and blocks the door and the driver's view; standees stay behind the line.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a speed threshold; when standees are allowed, the rule is their position behind the standee line, not a speed cutoff.

options.a: Sits in the aisle when the overhead racks are full
options.b: Does not block aisles or exits and is secured against falling
options.c: Is placed next to the emergency exit where riders can reach it
options.d: Is stacked in the stepwell behind the closed front door

distractorExplanations.a: Aisle baggage creates a trip hazard and blocks evacuation; overflow goes into the baggage compartment, not the aisle.
distractorExplanations.c: Nothing may block access to an emergency exit; baggage beside the exit delays evacuation.
distractorExplanations.d: The stepwell must stay clear for boarding and evacuation; baggage there blocks the main exit and the driver's door.

options.a: Help them board, then move off before they are seated to keep schedule
options.b: Lift the passenger's wheelchair up the steps if the lift is slow to deploy
options.c: Allow adequate boarding time and use lifts/securement per training and rules
options.d: Secure the wheelchair with its own wheel brakes while the rider holds a stanchion

distractorExplanations.a: Moving before elderly or disabled riders are seated invites falls; give adequate time to be seated or secured first.
distractorExplanations.b: Carrying a wheelchair up the steps risks injury to rider and driver; the lift exists for this and is used per training.
distractorExplanations.d: Wheelchair brakes are not securement; the vehicle's approved tiedowns and occupant restraint are required.

options.a: Show where standing passengers must hold a stanchion while moving
options.b: Mark the minimum distance riders must wait back from the curb before boarding
options.c: Divide reserved priority seating from general seating on the bus
options.d: Keep passengers from entering the area that would block the driver’s view

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the standee line with a handhold zone; its purpose is keeping riders out of the area that blocks the driver.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes a curbside boarding line, not the standee line marked on the bus floor near the driver.
distractorExplanations.c: Priority seating is marked with signs, not the standee line; the line restricts standing in the driver's area.

cdl-passenger-readiness-check-loading-pa.explanation: Forward of the standee line is restricted for safety/visibility; riders there would block the driver's view or access to controls.

options.a: Ensure doors are closed, passengers are clear of doorways, and the path is safe
options.b: Close the doors and pull away once the last rider has paid the fare
options.c: Check the right-side mirror and pull out, reopening the doors if anyone calls out
options.d: Rely on the brake-door interlock to show it is safe to move

distractorExplanations.b: Paying the fare does not mean the rider is clear of the doorway or seated; clearance is confirmed before moving.
distractorExplanations.c: Reacting after someone calls out is too late; doors, doorway clearance and the path are confirmed before the bus moves.
distractorExplanations.d: A brake-door interlock does not confirm passengers are clear of the doorway or path; the driver still checks mirrors.

options.a: Direct them to move so the exit remains usable
options.b: Let them stay if they promise to move in an emergency
options.c: Allow it while the bus is moving, then clear it at stops
options.d: Ask them to sit on the floor beside the exit instead

distractorExplanations.b: Exits stay clear at all times; waiting for an emergency to clear the space costs critical evacuation seconds.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the risk: the exit must be clear while moving, when a crash or fire could require immediate evacuation.
distractorExplanations.d: Sitting on the floor beside the exit still obstructs it and leaves an unsecured rider; they should take a seat elsewhere.

options.a: Using two front tiedowns with the chair brakes set, since rear straps are meant for scooters
options.b: Using the vehicle’s approved straps/tiedowns at designated points and passenger restraint as required
options.c: Using the wheelchair's own lap belt as the occupant restraint, adding floor tiedowns on highway trips
options.d: Using the vehicle's straps at any convenient frame point, with the chair facing sideways in the aisle

distractorExplanations.a: Securement uses four points (two front, two rear) plus occupant restraint; rear straps are needed for every wheelchair, not just scooters.
distractorExplanations.c: A chair's postural belt is not a crash-rated occupant restraint, and floor tiedowns are used on every trip, not just highway runs.
distractorExplanations.d: Straps go to designated securement points and the chair faces forward in the securement area; sideways aisle placement is unsafe.

cdl-passenger-readiness-check-loading-pa.explanation: Manufacturers and regs specify securement systems—follow them, with brakes set as appropriate and the occupant restraint applied.

options.a: It mainly causes fare-collection delays that push the bus off schedule
options.b: It voids the bus warranty, which is why capacity plates are posted
options.c: It blocks aisles/exits, increases tip/weight issues, and slows evacuation
options.d: It shortens stopping distance by adding tire traction, but crowds the driver

distractorExplanations.a: Schedule delay is not the safety reason; overloading blocks exits, overloads axles and slows evacuation.
distractorExplanations.b: Capacity limits are safety limits for weight and egress, not warranty conditions.
distractorExplanations.d: Added weight lengthens stopping distance and stresses the brakes; it does not improve stopping.

options.a: Passengers can stand and move to the door before the bus stops
options.b: The driver meets the fare-audit rule for logging each stop
options.c: Riders can gather in the stepwell so the stop takes less time
options.d: Passengers can prepare to exit safely without sudden movement

distractorExplanations.a: Riders stay seated until the bus stops; announcements give time to gather belongings, not to stand while moving.
distractorExplanations.b: Announcements are about rider safety and preparation, not an audit or logging requirement.
distractorExplanations.c: The stepwell must stay clear while moving; gathering there exposes riders to falls when the bus brakes.

options.a: Service animals and other animals only as permitted by policy/law
options.b: Pets of any size, provided the owner keeps them on a short leash
options.c: Service animals carrying an official ID card or vest as proof
options.d: Small pets in carriers, with service animals placed in the baggage bay

distractorExplanations.b: Carrier policy limits non-service animals; a leash alone does not authorize pets of any size on board.
distractorExplanations.c: Under ADA rules service animals are not required to wear a vest or carry ID; demanding documentation is improper.
distractorExplanations.d: Service animals ride with their handler in the passenger area; they are not placed in the baggage compartment.

options.a: Mainly fare-box damage if drinks spill while riders pay at the front
options.b: Spills causing burns during acceleration/turns—encourage secure lids/seating
options.c: Riders spilling on themselves, which is their own responsibility to manage on board
options.d: Coffee steam fogging the windshield and reducing the driver's view

distractorExplanations.a: Fare-box damage is not the safety concern; hot spills burn riders during starts, stops and turns.
distractorExplanations.c: Smooth operation and lid/seating reminders by the driver reduce scald risk; it is part of passenger safety management.
distractorExplanations.d: Steam from cups does not meaningfully fog the windshield; the hazard is scald burns and slips during acceleration and turns.

options.a: Removing disruptive riders physically when they refuse to follow rules
options.b: Enforcing safety rules at terminals, leaving behavior on board to riders
options.c: Reasonable rules enforcement for safety without unnecessary escalation
options.d: Letting riders settle disputes among themselves while the bus keeps moving

distractorExplanations.a: Physical removal escalates risk; drivers enforce rules verbally and call law enforcement per company procedure.
distractorExplanations.b: The driver manages rider conduct on board too; safety rules apply throughout the trip, not just at terminals.
distractorExplanations.d: Disputes that affect safety need driver action—stop safely and get help; leaving them to riders invites escalation.

options.a: Stop, look, and listen as required for passenger vehicles—do not shift gears while crossing
options.b: Stop 5 to 10 feet from the nearest rail, look and listen, then shift gears midway across
options.c: Slow to 15 mph, look both ways, and cross without stopping when no train is visible
options.d: Stop when the lights are flashing, otherwise cross in a gear low enough to avoid shifting

distractorExplanations.b: Wrong stopping distance (the rule is 15 to 50 feet from the nearest rail), and gears are not shifted while crossing.
distractorExplanations.c: Buses carrying passengers come to a full stop 15 to 50 feet from the tracks; slowing and looking is not enough.
distractorExplanations.d: Passenger buses stop at public crossings even without active signals, unless an exempt sign or officer directs otherwise.

options.a: Keep passengers seated while you try to restart the engine for one minute
options.b: Evacuate passengers away from the tracks immediately and then contact authorities
options.c: Contact the railroad first so dispatch can stop the train, then evacuate
options.d: Evacuate passengers away from the tracks in the same direction the train is traveling

distractorExplanations.a: Restart attempts waste critical time; passengers are evacuated first, then the driver contacts authorities.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the sequence: everyone gets off and away from the tracks before any calls are made.
distractorExplanations.d: Moving in the train's direction of travel puts riders in the debris path; they go at an angle toward the direction the train is coming from.

options.a: Smooth driving mainly reduces fuel use and brake wear on long routes
options.b: Sudden stops matter only when standees are aboard; seated riders are safe
options.c: Sudden starts/stops injure standing passengers and cause falls
options.d: Passengers can brace for sudden stops if the driver honks first

distractorExplanations.a: Fuel and brake wear are side benefits; the safety reason is that sudden motion throws riders and causes falls.
distractorExplanations.b: Seated riders can also be thrown into seatbacks and the aisle; smooth operation protects everyone, not just standees.
distractorExplanations.d: Riders cannot reliably brace on a warning; smooth starts, stops and turns prevent falls in the first place.

options.a: Back slowly using mirrors alone, since a helper can block the camera view
options.b: Back at a steady moderate speed so the maneuver ends quickly in traffic
options.c: Have a passenger stand in the rear aisle to watch through the back window
options.d: Use a helper when possible, check mirrors, and back slowly the shortest distance

distractorExplanations.a: A helper is recommended when possible because mirrors leave blind areas directly behind the bus.
distractorExplanations.b: Backing is done as slowly as possible; speed cuts the time to react to someone in the blind area.
distractorExplanations.c: Rear windows show little of the area behind a bus; a helper outside the vehicle, in the driver's view, is needed.

options.a: Use the nearest safe exit and move to a safe assembly area away from traffic
options.b: Exit through the front door in seat order so the driver can count each of them
options.c: Wait at the bus door on the roadway side so the driver can find them
options.d: Take carry-on bags with them so belongings are not lost in a fire

distractorExplanations.b: Funneling everyone through one door slows evacuation; use the nearest safe exit and count at the assembly area.
distractorExplanations.c: The roadway side exposes riders to traffic; they move away from the bus and traffic to a safe assembly area.
distractorExplanations.d: Gathering belongings delays evacuation in fire or smoke; people leave items behind and get out.

options.a: Speeds above 50 mph; below that tires stay in full contact
options.b: Speed and standing water; reduce speed in rain
options.c: Low speed on wet roads, since tires need momentum to clear water
options.d: Overinflated tires; lowering pressure restores grip in rain

distractorExplanations.a: Hydroplaning can occur at speeds as low as 30 mph with enough water; there is no safe 50 mph floor.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the cause: higher speed lets water build under the tread; slowing down reduces hydroplaning.
distractorExplanations.d: Underinflated tires and worn tread make hydroplaning more likely; lowering pressure increases the risk.

options.a: Turn on hazards and wait 30 minutes before setting out triangles
options.b: Use hazards and keep passengers on the shoulder right beside the travel lane
options.c: Activate hazards, set out triangles, and keep passengers away from traffic
options.d: Set one triangle 10 feet behind the bus so drivers see it at once

distractorExplanations.a: Triangles go out as soon as possible, within 10 minutes of stopping; waiting 30 minutes leaves the bus unprotected.
distractorExplanations.b: Passengers belong well away from traffic, behind barriers if possible, not standing beside the travel lane.
distractorExplanations.d: Three triangles are placed at about 10, 100 and 100–200 feet depending on road type; one close triangle gives too little warning.

cdl-passenger-readiness-check-driving-ra.explanation: Visibility and separation from traffic prevent secondary crashes; set out triangles as required and keep evacuated passengers away from traffic.

options.a: Proceed carefully after stopping if no train is visible in either direction
options.b: Cross if the gates have been down for over 5 minutes with no train
options.c: Stop, then follow the vehicle ahead across once it clears the far rail
options.d: Do not cross—wait until it is safe and gates rise / signals allow

distractorExplanations.a: Lowered gates mean a train is coming or the crossing is closed; a clear view does not permit going around them.
distractorExplanations.b: A long wait does not authorize crossing; call the posted railroad number and wait for the gates to rise or an officer to direct you.
distractorExplanations.c: Following another vehicle does not make it safe; with gates down you stay stopped until the gates rise and signals clear.

options.a: Speed, brakes (avoid fade), and transmission use appropriate to the vehicle
options.b: Speed, by applying the service brakes lightly and steadily all the way down
options.c: Speed, by selecting a lower gear partway down once the bus picks up speed
options.d: Speed, by coasting in neutral and using the brakes as the bus speeds up

distractorExplanations.b: Light continuous braking overheats the brakes and causes fade; use a low gear with snub braking instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Select the low gear before starting down; trying to downshift once speed builds may leave you unable to get into gear.
distractorExplanations.d: Coasting removes engine braking and is prohibited; it makes the brakes do all the work and leads to fade.

options.a: Keep to the speed limit and use the vehicle ahead's taillights as a guide
options.b: Slow down, increase following distance, and use appropriate lighting
options.c: Slow down and switch to high beams so other drivers see you sooner
options.d: Slow down and pull onto the shoulder with only parking lights on

distractorExplanations.a: Following taillights gives a false sense of safety; speed must drop to what you can see, not stay at the limit.
distractorExplanations.c: High beams reflect off fog and reduce your own vision; low beams and fog lights are used.
distractorExplanations.d: If you must stop, get fully off the road and use hazard flashers; parking lights alone on a shoulder invite rear-end crashes.

options.a: Keep driving to the next scheduled stop and report the fight to dispatch there
options.b: Stop immediately in the travel lane and separate the fighters yourself
options.c: Stop in a safe place if needed, protect safety, and call for assistance per policy
options.d: Drive to the nearest police station without stopping, however far it is

distractorExplanations.a: A fight that endangers operation requires stopping safely now; waiting for the next stop prolongs the hazard.
distractorExplanations.b: Stopping in a travel lane creates a crash hazard and physical intervention escalates; stop in a safe place and call for help.
distractorExplanations.d: Continuing while violence affects safe operation risks a crash; stop safely first and request help to come to you.

options.a: Convex mirrors show the true distance of vehicles traveling alongside the bus
options.b: Signaling three seconds ahead clears the lane before you move over
options.c: The flat mirrors cover the whole area beside a bus with no gaps
options.d: Blind spots are large and passengers/vehicles can be hidden along the sides

distractorExplanations.a: Convex mirrors make objects look smaller and farther away than they are; they do not show true distance.
distractorExplanations.b: A signal warns others but does not create space; mirrors and a blind-spot check confirm the lane is clear.
distractorExplanations.c: Flat mirrors leave large blind areas along the sides; convex mirrors and head checks are needed too.

options.a: Stop and not cross until it is safe / signal allows
options.b: Slow down and cross if the span is still level and the gate is up
options.c: Stop if the bridge attendant waves you down personally
options.d: Cross promptly before the warning ends so you do not wait

distractorExplanations.b: When a signal requires a stop you stop even if the span looks level; the signal controls, not your own view.
distractorExplanations.c: A stop signal requires stopping by itself; you do not wait for an attendant's wave before obeying it.
distractorExplanations.d: Racing a drawbridge warning risks driving onto a moving span; obey the stop signal and wait.

options.a: It is required for the incident report filed within 24 hours
options.b: You must account for passengers and report missing persons to responders
options.c: Responders count passengers themselves, so the driver's count only speeds up paperwork
options.d: It lets you decide who may re-enter the bus to retrieve belongings

distractorExplanations.a: Paperwork is not the reason; the count tells responders right now whether anyone is still trapped aboard.
distractorExplanations.c: Responders rely on the driver's count to know if anyone is missing; it directs rescue, not paperwork.
distractorExplanations.d: No one re-enters an evacuated bus for belongings; the headcount exists to find missing people.

options.a: Opening the hood fully to reach the fire, then spraying the extinguisher at the flames
options.b: Keeping passengers aboard while you fight the fire, since exiting near traffic is riskier
options.c: Evacuating passengers, using extinguishers if safe/trained, and not opening the hood carelessly
options.d: Using water on the engine fire first, saving the extinguisher in case it spreads

distractorExplanations.a: Opening the hood feeds oxygen to the fire; aim through louvers or from below, at the base of the fire, not the flames.
distractorExplanations.b: Fire risk outweighs traffic exposure; evacuate passengers to a safe spot away from traffic before fighting the fire.
distractorExplanations.d: Water can spread fuel and electrical fires; use the extinguisher rated for the fire class, aimed at the base.

options.a: Prohibited / unsafe practice—discharge passengers before fueling
options.b: Allowed if the engine is running so the heat and AC stay on for riders
options.c: Acceptable in a closed garage as long as no one smokes near the pump
options.d: Permitted with riders aboard if the driver stays at the nozzle throughout

distractorExplanations.b: Fueling with the engine running is itself prohibited; it adds ignition risk on top of having riders aboard.
distractorExplanations.c: The CDL manual specifically warns against fueling in a closed building with riders aboard; vapors accumulate there.
distractorExplanations.d: Attending the nozzle is required anyway, but it does not make fueling with passengers aboard acceptable.

options.a: Allowed below 15 mph in stop-and-go city traffic
options.b: Prohibited because passengers can fall out
options.c: Allowed if passengers are seated behind the standee line
options.d: Permitted on short hops between nearby stops on a route

distractorExplanations.a: No low-speed allowance exists; an open door while moving lets riders fall out at any speed.
distractorExplanations.c: The standee line does not stop someone falling through an open door; doors stay closed while the bus moves.
distractorExplanations.d: Short distances between stops do not change the risk; doors are closed before moving every time.

options.a: Allowed when stopped at a red light or in slow traffic in the lane
options.b: Allowed if the call is kept under one minute and is dispatch-related
options.c: Generally prohibited under federal/state distracted driving rules for CDL drivers
options.d: Prohibited for texting, but hand-held talking remains legal for CDL drivers

distractorExplanations.a: FMCSA's hand-held ban covers driving, including when temporarily stopped in traffic or at a light; you must be off the road.
distractorExplanations.b: There is no short-call or dispatch exception; hands-free use, or calls to emergency services, are what is permitted.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the texting ban (49 CFR 392.80) with the separate hand-held phone ban (392.82); both apply to CMV drivers.

options.a: The same as for car drivers, with a 0.08 BAC limit on duty
options.b: Satisfied if the driver stops drinking two hours before duty
options.c: Met as long as alcohol stays sealed in the driver's personal bag while on duty
options.d: Strict—alcohol misuse endangers passengers and violates FMCSA alcohol rules

distractorExplanations.a: CDL holders in a CMV have a 0.04 BAC limit and are put out of service for 24 hours at any detectable amount.
distractorExplanations.b: Wrong timing: FMCSA bars alcohol use within 4 hours before going on duty, not 2.
distractorExplanations.c: Drivers may not possess alcohol while on duty unless it is manifested cargo; a personal bag still violates the rule.

options.a: Allowed for under 10 minutes with the engine running and doors open
options.b: Unsafe and often prohibited unless proper precautions are taken
options.c: Fine if the brake-door interlock is engaged instead of the parking brake
options.d: Acceptable if a passenger sits in the driver's seat to watch the controls

distractorExplanations.a: There is no 10-minute allowance; leaving riders aboard without setting the parking brake and securing the bus risks a rollaway.
distractorExplanations.c: The CDL manual says not to use the brake-door interlock in place of the parking brake when leaving the bus.
distractorExplanations.d: A passenger is not a substitute for securing the bus; untrained riders should not be left at the controls.

options.a: Allowed if pulling over would make the bus stop on a hill or curve
options.b: Acceptable on divided highways where emergency vehicles can pass
options.c: Illegal and especially dangerous with a busload of passengers
options.d: Required of cars, with buses exempt to protect standing riders

distractorExplanations.a: You still yield—slow, move right and stop as soon as it is safe; a hill or curve changes how you yield, not whether.
distractorExplanations.b: Yield and move-over laws apply on divided highways too; room for passing does not excuse failing to yield.
distractorExplanations.d: Buses have no exemption; drivers yield smoothly to avoid throwing riders, but they must yield.

options.a: Allowed in the passenger area as long as each package carries the correct hazard label
options.b: Allowed for poison gas and tear gas if sealed in the rear baggage compartment
options.c: Permitted when the driver also holds an H endorsement for hazardous materials work
options.d: Prohibited / tightly restricted—passenger operations are not general hazmat freighters

distractorExplanations.a: Labeled hazmat generally may not ride in the passenger space; small-arms ammunition and emergency hospital supplies are narrow exceptions.
distractorExplanations.b: Division 2.3 poison gas, liquid Class 6 poisons, tear gas and irritating materials may not be carried on a bus at all, baggage bay included.
distractorExplanations.c: The H endorsement covers placarded hazmat freight; it does not authorize forbidden hazmat on a passenger bus.

options.a: A paperwork error fixed by an amended log
options.b: Illegal and can disqualify drivers
options.c: Only a carrier violation, not the driver's
options.d: Permitted if an ELD malfunction loses data

distractorExplanations.a: Deliberate falsification is a violation, not an error; amending afterward does not cure knowingly false records.
distractorExplanations.c: Drivers who falsify records are personally liable and can face civil penalties and disqualification.
distractorExplanations.d: An ELD malfunction requires accurate paper logs as a backup; it does not permit recording false hours.

options.a: Bus speed governors fail above 65 mph, cutting engine power suddenly
options.b: Speed raises reaction distance but leaves braking distance unchanged
options.c: Stopping distance and crash severity rise dramatically with speed and load
options.d: A heavier bus stops shorter because added weight improves tire traction on the road

distractorExplanations.a: Governors limit top speed rather than failing; the danger is longer stopping distance and higher crash energy.
distractorExplanations.b: Speed increases both reaction and braking distance; doubling speed roughly quadruples braking distance.
distractorExplanations.d: More weight means more momentum and brake heat, so a loaded bus needs a longer stopping distance.

options.a: Allowed if you stay within the 11-hour driving limit for the day
options.b: Allowed with the dispatcher's approval when no relief driver exists
options.c: Managed by a 30-minute break, which resets fitness for duty
options.d: Prohibited—out-of-service illness/fatigue rules protect the public

distractorExplanations.a: Passenger carriers have a 10-hour driving limit, and 49 CFR 392.3 bars driving while impaired by fatigue or illness at any point.
distractorExplanations.b: Section 392.3 also bars carriers from requiring or permitting an impaired driver to drive; dispatch approval changes nothing.
distractorExplanations.c: The 30-minute break is a property-carrier hours item and does not cure illness or fatigue that makes driving unsafe.

options.a: Extremely dangerous and must be avoided by ensuring space to clear fully
options.b: Acceptable if the bus rear overhangs the rail by less than 3 feet
options.c: Acceptable if you stop with your hazards on so the train crew sees you
options.d: Unavoidable in traffic, so wait on the tracks until the cars ahead move

distractorExplanations.b: Trains are wider than the rails; any part of the bus inside the track zone can be struck, so the bus must clear fully.
distractorExplanations.c: A train cannot stop quickly; hazard lights do not protect a bus stopped across the tracks.
distractorExplanations.d: You do not start across until there is room on the far side; waiting on the tracks for traffic is exactly the hazard.

options.a: Allowed if the detector is turned off while on duty
options.b: Against FMCSA rules for CMVs in interstate commerce
options.c: Restricted to night driving under FMCSA rules
options.d: Banned by some states, with no federal CMV rule

distractorExplanations.a: 49 CFR 392.71 bars even having a radar detector in the CMV; switching it off does not comply.
distractorExplanations.c: The federal radar-detector ban for CMVs applies at all hours, not just at night.
distractorExplanations.d: FMCSA's 392.71 bans radar detectors in CMVs federally, on top of any state rules.

options.a: Allowed on the shoulder when traffic ahead is stopped and the lane is clear
options.b: Acceptable when dispatch confirms the route is behind schedule
options.c: Unsafe, often illegal, and inconsistent with passenger carrier responsibilities
options.d: A minor traffic issue that matters for cars more than for buses

distractorExplanations.a: Passing on the shoulder is illegal in most places and dangerous with a loaded bus; wait for traffic to move.
distractorExplanations.b: Schedule pressure does not authorize reckless maneuvers; passenger safety comes before on-time performance.
distractorExplanations.d: A bus's size, weight and passenger load make reckless maneuvers more dangerous, not less.
